ocean3d

ocean3d is an R package for three-dimensional marine spatial analysis of species ranges, fisheries, and depth-stratified oceanographic data. It grew out of work on sharks, rays, and chimaeras, with the functions generalising to any marine taxon or spatial layer.

The three-dimensional marine environment poses a unique challenge for spatial analyses. Most conventional GIS workflows represent space as a two-dimensional plane. This abstraction fails to capture the range of depths and vertical overlap of marine habitat. Fisheries also operate at different depths depending on gear type and target species, creating depth-specific patterns of threat exposure that require analysis in 3D volume rather than 2D planes to quantify. ocean3d provides documented workflows and reusable functions for:

  • extracting values from depth-stratified oceanographic rasters within user-defined geographic areas and depth windows;
  • characterising the abiotic habitat (e.g., temperature, dissolved oxygen) of marine species using IUCN Red List ranges and World Ocean Atlas 2023 climatologies;
  • calculating three-dimensional overlap between species distributions, fisheries effort, and other spatial layers;
  • producing depth-aware maps and depth-profile plots of species ranges, environmental conditions, and cumulative fishing pressure.

How it works

Species ranges and other spatial layers are usually stored as 2D maps, but marine species and activities also occupy a depth range, bounded by the seafloor. ocean3d combines a 2D range, a depth range, bathymetry and gridded environmental data into one 3D representation, so you can ask, for example, which temperatures occur within a species’ 3D distribution.

A species’ range as a 2D polygon on a bathymetry map (A) and as a 3D distribution between the surface and the seafloor in a vertical cross-section (B). Panel C shows the inputs ocean3d combines: the range polygon, the depth range, bathymetry and temperature at several depths, to find the temperatures within the 3D distribution.

In order to represent the 3D space in the ocean, we use a stacked-raster approach built on terra. We call this the Spatial Voxel Model, with the class SpatVoxel. Using this SpatVoxel, we can represent any number of spatial phenomena in the ocean, including species distributions, fishing effort, and oceanographic variables.

ocean3d has three representations for 3D geometry:

  • A SpatVector3D holds points, lines and polygons with depth and time, such as tag detections, dive tracks or a protected area from 0 to 200 m. Each polygon has a top and a bottom depth. Build one with as_vector3d().
  • A SpatEnvelope stores one continuous [depth_min, depth_max] interval per grid cell, bounded by the seafloor. It suits ranges with defined limits in area and depth, such as IUCN species ranges and fishery footprints.
  • A SpatVoxel stores a value at each of a set of depth levels in every cell. It suits continuous values, such as temperature or the modelled probability of occurrence, and can hold interior gaps and overhangs, because it has a value at every depth rather than one depth range.
The same example as a SpatVector3D, a polygon with a top and bottom surface (A); a SpatEnvelope, its depth_min and depth_max on a grid above the seafloor (B); and a SpatVoxel, presence at depth levels from 50 to 500 m (C). The curved top and bottom surfaces and vector3d_to_envelope() are planned: a SpatVector3D polygon currently has one depth range.

vector3d_to_envelope() and the curved top and bottom surfaces in panel A are planned. Today each SpatVector3D polygon has one depth range.

Functions convert between these representations. vect_to_envelope() turns a species range polygon and its observed depth range into a SpatEnvelope bounded by the seafloor, and envelope_to_voxel() places it on the depth levels of a SpatVoxel, as in panels B and C above.

This package includes utilities for working with commonly used datasets in marine habitat spatial analyses, including IUCN Red List, World Ocean Atlas, GEBCO, Copernicus Marine, and Global Fishing Watch.

Existing spatial analysis packages and their limitations

Several R packages and other tools handle depth or 3D data, and ocean3d builds on terra, sf, ncdf4 and CFtime. None of the tools below answers 3D spatial queries on gridded marine data on its own: which cells and depths a species, fishery or other layer occupies above the seafloor, where two of them overlap in 3D, and what environmental values fall inside.

Tool What it does Limitations for 3D spatial analysis
terra Raster and vector analysis. A multi-layer SpatRaster can record one depth per layer with terra::depth(). Functions such as mask(), extract() and zonal() treat layers as a stack and don’t use their depths. A raster can’t store a depth range per cell, and there is no 3D intersect, overlap or volume. In our trial, terra read 19 of 29 netCDF test cases correctly, and its errors were silent.
sf Vector geometry and spatial queries (buffers, clips, intersections). Geometries can carry Z coordinates, but operations such as st_intersection(), st_buffer() and st_area() work in 2D and ignore them. No raster data.
stars Arrays with any number of dimensions (data cubes), including depth and time. No class for a depth range per cell, and no 3D intersect or volume. In our trial, extracting 2 points from a large file through a stars proxy took 198–243 s or tried to allocate 51–56 GB, and slicing a proxy dropped the decoded time.
rgl, rayshader 3D visualisation. They draw 3D scenes. They don’t do spatial queries or calculate volumes.
lidR, rTLS 3D point clouds from LiDAR and terrestrial laser scanning. Built for dense point clouds of land surfaces and vegetation. They don’t work on gridded ocean data with depth levels, a seafloor and time.
PostGIS 3D functions on vector geometry in a PostgreSQL database. Its 3D functions are for vector geometry, and its rasters have bands but no depth. Using it means running a database outside R.

Installation

You can install the development version of ocean3d from GitHub with:

# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("Marine-Biodiversity-Conservation-Lab/ocean3d")

Function overview

An analysis in ocean3d has three steps: build 3D objects from your inputs, intersect them with each other or with the data, and summarise the result as volumes, overlaps or statistics. The functions below are grouped by step (see the package design in SPEC.md).

Which input each function takes

ocean3d currently has two data models for gridded data, and each function takes one of them:

Input Functions Reads with
netCDF files (paths, open ncdf4 connections or a file table) extract_to_point() and its extract2d() / extract3d_*() wrappers, extract_to_buffer(), extract_to_track() ncdf4, only the cells each observation needs; keeps the time dimension
SpatVoxel / SpatEnvelope (3D classes built on terra::SpatRaster) the build, intersect and volume functions, mask() and extract_to_area() terra; no time dimension

The two don’t convert into each other yet. A voxel from woa_load_nc() and as_voxel() can’t be passed to extract_to_point(), and a netCDF file can’t be passed to extract_to_area() or volume(). To use a netCDF file with the voxel functions, load it as a SpatRaster (e.g. with woa_load_nc()) and wrap it with as_voxel(). Merging the two into one model with time is planned in #99. The first, experimental part of that model is as_proxy(). It describes one variable of a netCDF file as a SpatProxy without reading its values. No other function accepts a SpatProxy yet.

Build: 3D objects

Input: SpatRaster layers, tables of points or lines, and polygons (sf, SpatVector). Output: SpatVoxel, SpatEnvelope or SpatVector3D.

  • create_study_raster() — build an empty study-area SpatRaster covering the combined extent of one or more spatial inputs.
  • as_voxel() — wrap a multi-depth SpatRaster (or a list of single-depth ones) as a validated SpatVoxel, ordered shallow to deep, with each layer’s depth in terra::depth(). This is how gridded data, including netCDF files described with as_proxy() or loaded with terra, enter the voxel model.
  • as_envelope() — define a 3D envelope with two rasters, with depth_min and depth_max corresponding to the minimum and maximum depths present in given cell.
  • as_vector3d() — build a SpatVector3D of points, lines or polygons with depth and time, from a table with one row per vertex or from sf or SpatVector geometry.
  • vect_to_envelope() — rasterize a single species range or fishery footprint onto the study grid and attach per-cell depth_min / depth_max, returning a SpatEnvelope.
  • envelope_to_voxel() — expand an envelope onto a set of depth levels. profile_flat() and profile_equal() set how a cell’s value is spread down the levels it occupies.
  • voxel_to_envelope() — collapse a voxel to the envelope bounding it, using a predicate on the cell values. Lossy: interior gaps are filled.
  • occupied() — turn a voxel of values (e.g. temperature) into a presence voxel, using a predicate on the cell values.
  • depths() — read the depth of each layer of a voxel.

Intersect: 3D spatial query

Input: SpatVoxel or SpatEnvelope, compared with another 3D object or a 2D one: a SpatRaster footprint or polygons (SpatVector, sf). A 2D object restricts the domain horizontally without restricting the depths.

  • intersect_3d(x, y) — the shared 3D space between the two inputs. Returns an envelope with the shared depth interval or a presence voxel, depending on inputs.
  • intersects_3d(x, y) — whether inputs share any 3D space, cell by cell: TRUE, FALSE (both present but disjoint, or only one present), or NA (neither present).
  • mask(x, mask) — terra::mask() made depth-aware. Keeps the values of x where the mask domain reaches that cell at that depth.

Summarise: 3D volume

Input: SpatEnvelope or SpatVoxel. A voxel’s volume sums the slab each occupied depth level stands for, so interior gaps cost volume instead of being filled in.

  • volume() — 3D volume (km³) of a rasterized domain, as a total or per cell (per_cell = TRUE). Measure an overlap with volume(intersect_3d(a, b)).

Summarise: environmental extraction from a SpatVoxel

Input: a SpatVoxel already loaded with terra.

  • extract_to_area() — crop a SpatVoxel to an area polygon and select layers within a depth range.
  • mask() (above) — keep a SpatVoxel‘s values inside a 3D volume, such as a species’ range from vect_to_envelope().

See vignette("ocean3d") for the full workflow, from a range polygon through to a vertical profile of the values inside it.

Summarise: environmental extraction from netCDF files

Input: observations (data frame, tibble, sf POINT, matrix, or named list) and one or more netCDF files. These functions read the files directly, only the cells each observation needs, and match time as well as depth. They don’t take a SpatVoxel.

  • extract_to_point() — the general engine: match observation points against one or more netCDF files. By default a point takes the value of the grid cell that contains it (NA outside the grid); spatial_match = "nearest" accepts the nearest cell centre within max_distance_km. Time is matched to the nearest timestamp and depth by physical depth in metres. Returns the input with the extracted values appended, structure preserved.
  • extract2d() — for variables with no depth dimension.
  • extract3d_nearest() — the valid, non-missing depth layer closest to each observation’s depth, so a cell below the seabed does not silently return NA.
  • extract3d_surface() / extract3d_bottom() — the physically shallowest depth layer, or the deepest non-missing one at that cell.
  • extract3d_all() — nearest, surface and bottom in one pass, as three columns.
  • extract_to_buffer() — summarise values within a geodesic circle × depth window × time window around each observation, weighted by cell coverage, layer thickness and time, or pick the value closest to a target.
  • extract_to_track() — sample points along ordered tracks (e.g. tagging data), extract values at them, and optionally summarise per track.

Data utilities

These download or load public datasets. The loaders return a plain SpatRaster; wrap it with as_voxel() or as_envelope() to use it with the build, intersect and volume functions above. The netCDF extraction functions take the downloaded files themselves (e.g. from woa_download()).

IUCN Red List API utilities

Add an IUCN Red List API key to access species-assessment functions. Sign up and acquire your API key at https://api.iucnredlist.org/:

usethis::edit_r_environ()
# Add the following line to the .Renviron file
# IUCN_REDLIST_KEY="your_iucn_api_key_here"
  • fetch_species_assessments() — query the IUCN Red List API for taxonomy, Red List category, and depth limits, by SIS ID, scientific name, or comprehensive group code.
  • fill_missing_depths() — fix swapped upper/lower depth values and fill missing values from genus-level means.

GEBCO Bathymetry

  • load_gebco_bathymetry() — load a GEBCO bathymetry NetCDF as a SpatRaster.

World Ocean Atlas 2023 utilities

  • woa_download() — download WOA 2023 NetCDF files (temperature, salinity, dissolved oxygen, oxygen saturation, AOU, nitrate, phosphate, silicate, density) at 0.25°, 1°, or 5° resolution, with caching.
  • woa_load_nc() — load a WOA NetCDF and select a statistical field (e.g., objectively analyzed climatology), returning a SpatRaster with one layer per depth, for as_voxel().
  • woa_cache_dir() / woa_cache_clear() — manage the persistent WOA download cache.

Global Fishing Watch (fisheries effort)

  • gfw_effort_to_raster() — turn the long-format apparent-fishing-hours tibble from gfwr::gfw_ais_fishing_hours() into a multi-layer SpatRaster, one layer per gear (or other grouping). Extending that into 3D uses the general converters — as_envelope() and envelope_to_voxel() — driven by a gear-to-depth-band lookup. Those operating-depth priors are analysis assumptions rather than package data, so they live in the gfw-fishing-effort-3d article.

Use of generative AI

Generative AI tools were used to write much of this package. This section says how, following rOpenSci’s AI policy.

  • Without AI: the package grew out of analysis scripts written over about three years without AI, for a study of 3D overlap between species and fisheries in Bangladesh (thesis) and for extracting environmental variables per species (preprint). The first version of the package, including the first SPEC.md, tests and documentation, was written by hand from those scripts.
  • With AI: since then, most of the code, tests and documentation have been written with generative AI tools, mainly Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI GPT 6.1 Sol. AI is also used to review code and to draw some of the figures in the documentation.
  • What the authors do: decide the package design (for example the SpatVoxel and SpatEnvelope classes, the build, intersect and summarise steps, and the data model decisions in SPEC.md), decide what each issue should do, and review every pull request before it is merged.
  • How contributions are made: CONTRIBUTING.md and AGENTS.md set the rules AI agents follow. Commits and pull requests written with an agent name the model in a Co-Authored-By: trailer.

Contributing

Contributions are welcome. ocean3d is being actively built out from a set of lab analyses into a general, tested package, and there is plenty of well-scoped work available. Start with:

  • CONTRIBUTING.md — development setup, data requirements, the branching/coordination workflow, and coding conventions.
  • SPEC.md — the roadmap; every planned function with its priority and source. Unchecked items are up for grabs.
  • Code of Conduct.

New contributors: the “Known rough edges / good first issues” section of CONTRIBUTING.md lists concrete starting points.
